title: Strict liability — Rylands v Fletcher and Indian developments

content.overview: Strict liability in tort, rooted in Rylands v Fletcher as received in India, makes a person who brings onto land and keeps something likely to do mischief if it escapes liable for the natural consequences of escape, without proof of negligence, subject to recognised exceptions; Indian courts have also articulated absolute liability in hazardous-enterprise contexts.
content.study: Identify non-natural use, a dangerous thing, escape, and damage. Apply classic exceptions (act of God, plaintiff's default, consent, act of stranger, statutory authority) carefully. Distinguish Rylands strict liability from M.C. Mehta absolute liability for hazardous industries, where defences are far narrower. Contrast with negligence, which turns on fault.
